10.1016/j.cag.2026.104734.title: Primal–dual polycatenanes: Modular design and construction of catenated 3D graphs from labeled 3-honeycombs and their duals
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104734.abstract: In this paper, we present a methodology for the design and construction of fully connected catenated 3D graphs. The central idea is to use labeled cell-transitive 3-honeycombs as geometric and combinatorial scaffolds for generating mechanically interlocked graph embeddings. Starting from a labeled honeycomb, we derive corresponding primal and dual spatial graphs whose embeddings are inherited from the underlying honeycomb structure. The primal–dual relationship provides a combinatorial scaffold from which mechanically interlocked structures can be systematically constructed while reducing the design problem to the construction and labeling of periodic honeycombs. A key feature of the methodology is the introduction of periodic domains as modular building blocks. Different labeling schemes generate different periodic domains, allowing the systematic creation of distinct polycatenane assemblies while preserving the underlying crystallographic structure. Since the framework is based on cell-transitive 3-honeycombs, it can be applied uniformly to broad families of crystallographic structures. We demonstrate the approach on several examples and present additive-manufacturing results that confirm the physical realizability of the generated polycatenanes.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104747.title: Steering the transition: A visual analytics approach to interactive energy scenario modeling
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104747.abstract: Navigating the transition to net-zero requires energy planners to rapidly assess and contrast the impacts of competing policy decisions. While computational models excel at large-scale optimization, they often lack the context to navigate the nuanced trade-offs and conflicting priorities of public policy. To bridge this gap, we present a visual analytics system that integrates human-in-the-loop expertise into the planning process, ensuring data-driven insights are tempered by practical judgment. Our approach introduces a modular planning paradigm designed to reduce the cognitive load of balancing multi-objective goals. Building upon previous work in human-in-the-loop decarbonization platforms, we present a visualization framework using model-driven glyphs to provide a consistent representation of multivariate data across geographic scales, ensuring an equitable assessment of interventions. Finally, we provide a tightly integrated workflow that allows planners to move fluidly between composing interventions, simulating decarbonization impacts, and performing cross-scenario comparisons. Through a detailed application scenario, we illustrate how this system accelerates the sensemaking process, allowing planners to benchmark strategies and deliver evidence-based policies with confidence.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104652.title: Approximating Doo–Sabin limit surfaces using geometrically continuous Bézier patchesImage 999
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104652.abstract: We present an efficient, globally G 1 –continuous scheme for extracting Bézier patches from any mesh with valence-four vertices and polygonal faces, that is, the mesh topology that arises in Doo-Sabin subdivision. The Bézier points are given explicitly as local, weighted averages in the vicinity of each vertex of the mesh, yielding bi-quadratic patches in regular regions and bi-quartic or bi-quintic patches in the vicinity of irregular regions. In particular, we first derive simple bi-quadratic averaging masks that produce quadratic patches that join with C 1 continuity in regular regions. In the vicinity of irregular faces, we elevate the degree, then impose certain symmetric gluing data of degree two on the patch interfaces, and compute explicitly masks as solution of the G 1 constraints. The resulting scheme, named G 1 ADS, ensures machine precision adherence to the G 1 conditions, reproduces quadratic C 1 B-splines at the regular regions, and enjoys a minimal number of degree elevated patches in the vicinity of irregular regions. We evaluate the performance of G 1 ADS quantitatively and qualitatively on several challenging benchmarks, in terms of accuracy, curvature and isophote analysis, and we compare with the state-of-the-art method. Our results demonstrate that G 1 ADS is efficient, robust and more accurate, producing high quality surfaces that converge to the respective Doo-Sabin limit surface.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104684.title: SfM-free 3D Gaussian Splatting from extremely sparse view
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104684.abstract: The effectiveness of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) depends on dense multi-view inputs and accurate camera poses. However, in real-world applications such as virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), capturing a large set of well-calibrated views is often impractical, and these requirements are thus difficult to satisfy. State-of-the-art approaches in sparse-view 3DGS typically estimate camera poses using structure-from-motion (SfM), which can fail under extremely settings and result in unreliable poses and weak geometries. In this work, we propose an SfM-free 3DGS framework that jointly estimates camera poses and reconstructs scene geometry from sparse input views. Our approach first employs a dense stereo module for robust initialization, generating both camera poses and a global dense point cloud. To mitigate the lack of intermediate-view supervision, a coherent view interpolation module synthesizes intermediate pseudo-views as auxiliary supervision. We further introduce two regularizers (LAC/PSG) to refine structural details and enhance rendering fidelity. Experiments show that our method outperforms existing 3DGS-based approaches, achieving a remarkable 2.75 dB improvement in PSNR under extremely sparse-view conditions (with only 2 training views). These advances make our approach suitable for real-world applications that demand high-quality rendering but lacks dense calibrated views.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104685.title: A double-covered probabilistic ray-based neural shape representation
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104685.abstract: Solutions to visual computing problems such as shape reconstruction, analysis, generation, and retrieval rely on fast and task-appropriate 3D shape representations for efficiency. This work explores representing shapes with neural ray fields, which are inherently more efficient to render than 3D coordinate-based neural representations requiring only a single network evaluation per ray, but with high data requirements and reduced fidelity thus far. We propose an improved ray field representation with improved gradient flow and a more tractable parameter domain, along with a more stable objective function and data augmentation improving stability and fidelity. We study the strengths and failure modes of the prior art and our method, and how performance scales with data and compute.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104704.title: A multimodal 2D–3D framework for façade window segmentation in urban scenes
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104704.abstract: Window detection on building façades is a relevant task for several applications in urban mapping, 3D city modelling, building characterisation and semantic annotation, e.g., for energy performance assessment. However, façade windows remain difficult to identify reliably in real urban scenes. Image-based methods can achieve good segmentation performance, but they may still suffer from occlusions or produce false positives on urban objects with a window-like appearance, such as vehicle windshields. Conversely, methods operating directly on point clouds or meshes suffer from poor acquisition of transparent surfaces, which typically result in sparse or incomplete 3D data. In this paper, we propose a multimodal framework combining a learning-based window segmentation on spherical imagery with semantic filtering on a 3D point cloud reconstructed from the same images. The key idea is to exploit the semantic and geometric consistency of the 3D scene to validate image-based segmentation and reject candidates that do not belong to building façades, exploiting the complementary strengths of 2D visual information and 3D semantic-geometric context. The proposed framework is evaluated on a street-level urban dataset acquired in Catania. Experimental results show that the proposed 3D validation stage significantly improves the reliability of the segmentation, reducing false positives by more than 50% and increasing precision from 0.58 to 0.70, while preserving competitive overall segmentation performance. In addition to the proposed pipeline, we introduce a new manually annotated dataset derived from spherical street-level acquisitions in Catania.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104707.title: Adaptive meshing of non-manifold parametric patch complexes with shared-curve compatibilityImage 999
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104707.abstract: We present an adaptive meshing technique for non-manifold parametric patch complexes with explicit shared curves. The method assumes that these shared curves are explicit entities of the input topology and preserves their discretization during refinement. Starting from a coarse patch-consistent mesh, each iteration evaluates curvature mismatch, updates patch- and curve-level refinement factors, rediscretizes shared curves, and rebuilds triangular patch interiors in the parametric domain using a hybrid quadtree-guided and advancing-front strategy. Shared-curve samples are stored once and reused by all incident patches, including curves incident to three or more patches, which preserves boundary compatibility by construction. Beyond this invariant, the technique integrates factor-driven curvature adaptation, conservative curve-level refinement, quadtree-supported interior sizing, and feature-aware advancing-front reconstruction to obtain compatible triangular patch meshes. The method is evaluated using normalized global error, triangle-shape quality, and a compatibility metric used to verify the shared-curve invariant and to compare against unsynchronized baselines. Across three evaluation cases, the approach reduces normalized global error by 74% to 96% while maintaining zero mean compatibility error. Controlled internal comparisons indicate that shared-curve synchronization is the mechanism responsible for boundary coherence, whereas hybrid reconstruction provides the strongest geometric improvement. The results support compatibility-preserving adaptive rebuilding as a practical strategy for controlled planar, curved, and mixed non-manifold patch configurations that satisfy explicit patch–curve assumptions.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104696.title: Does color resolve symmetry ambiguities in 3D point cloud registration? Literature survey and adversarial testing
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104696.abstract: Three-dimensional point cloud registration is a fundamental task in computer vision and robotics, and over the past three decades, many methods have explored how color information can improve alignment accuracy. Despite this, no survey has systematically examined how color is integrated into registration pipelines or the design decisions involved in this integration. We address this gap by collecting and classifying color-aware rigid 3D registration methods published in the last three decades. For each group, we provide a taxonomy, a timeline, and a discussion of key design choices and trade-offs. We also analyze, across the groups, how color strengthens each part of the registration problem and where it introduces new failure modes. A recurring claim in the literature is that color resolves geometric ambiguities, particularly on symmetric surfaces where geometry alone cannot constrain the pose. To test this claim, we assembled a focused evaluation on symmetric, textured objects and evaluated seven publicly available methods under controlled overlap and initialization conditions. The results reveal that the relationship between color and registration success is more nuanced than the literature suggests.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104713.title: Statuario-40k: Fine-tuning SAM 3 for instance segmentation at scale of monuments, statues, and cracks
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104713.abstract: Among the diverse pathologies that compromise the structural integrity of historical monuments, statues, and masonry infrastructures, surface cracking is a primary indicator of both localised material fatigue and systemic structural distress. However, instance segmentation of cultural heritage artefacts remains bottlenecked by annotation scarcity, strong geometric variability in sculptural forms, heterogeneous materials, scales, and preservation states, and the limited cultural breadth and variety of existing benchmarks. Moreover, instance segmentation of cracked statues and monuments is especially challenging because the fine-grained and unpredictable geometry of structural damage further complicates reliable annotation. In this paper we present Statuario-40k , a 39,280-image dataset and training pipeline for instance segmentation of monuments, statues, columns, and pedestals in challenging heritage imagery. Our key idea is to turn publicly available clean monument videos into a scalable pseudo-labelling data flywheel using the standard public SAM 3 video model with temporal disambiguation and to complement fixed prompt banks with a second, VLM-guided prompt discovery stage that mines video-specific three-word prompts. Starting from 247,286 video frames extracted from YouTube, we retain 37,643 video-derived images after prompt pruning, COCO-format merging, and instance de-duplication; we then add 1537 curated web images from Bing and Kaggle to obtain the final dataset. We further collapse heterogeneous prompt strings into four canonical heritage classes and fine-tune an image-only SAM 3 model by freezing the visual backbone while updating the segmentation head and only four layers of the language encoder, reducing GPU memory requirements. Finally, we propose a depth-aware crack synthesis pipeline that injects material-compatible defects from OmniCrack30k into clean heritage imagery by exploiting both the monocular depth estimates from Depth Anything and the semantic information already available in the dataset. This synthesis stage converts clean heritage images into crack-aware training data with depth- and semantics-consistent defect placement, enabling the training of models that detect and segment crack instances on cultural heritage structures. We provide the full methodological pipeline and implementation and training details, as well as quantitative and qualitative evaluation protocols for both heritage object and crack instance segmentation. The dataset is available for download at this link: http://deeplearning.ge.imati.cnr.it/statuario-40k .

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104715.title: Style-aware gloss control for generative non-photorealistic rendering
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104715.abstract: Humans can infer material characteristics of objects from their visual appearance, and this ability extends to artistic depictions, where similar perceptual strategies guide the interpretation of paintings or drawings. Among the factors that define material appearance, gloss, along with color, is widely regarded as one of the most important, and recent studies indicate that humans can perceive gloss independently of the artistic style used to depict an object. To investigate how gloss and artistic style are represented in learned models, we train an unsupervised generative model on a newly curated dataset of painterly objects designed to systematically vary such factors. Our analysis reveals a hierarchical latent space in which gloss is disentangled from other appearance factors, allowing for a detailed study of how gloss is represented and varies across artistic styles. Building on this representation, we introduce a lightweight adapter that connects our style- and gloss-aware latent space to a latent-diffusion model, enabling the synthesis of non-photorealistic images with fine-grained control of these factors. We compare our approach with previous models and observe improved disentanglement and controllability of the learned factors.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104721.title: SAFHDR: Single-exposure HDR reconstruction via attention-guided feature learning and global information aggregation
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104721.abstract: The reconstruction of High Dynamic Range (HDR) images from a single Low Dynamic Range (LDR) image is a challenging problem in computer vision. State-of-the-art methods still have limitations in recovering regions degraded by severe clipping and noise in overexposed and underexposed areas. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes SAFHDR, a U-Net-based architecture composed of DAMU-Net, which incorporates deformable convolutions guided by the Optimized Attention Block and efficient multiscale processing via the Lightweight Residual Features Block, and the Information Aggregation Module, dedicated to preserving the global structure of the scene. Additionally, a two-stage training strategy is adopted to improve perceptual fidelity and suppress chromatic and structural artifacts. Experiments conducted on the NTIRE 2021 dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on HDR-oriented perceptual metrics, with high detail recovery capability in critical regions.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104730.title: Stabilizing joint rotation selection in skinning decomposition for high-fidelity facial auto rigging

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104728.title: ConGAT: Context-aware graph attention network for 3D region of interest discovery in multiplexed microscopy images
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104728.abstract: We present ConGAT, CON text-aware G raph AT tention Network, a visual analysis system for identifying and analyzing cell–cell interactions in large tissue volumes, which leverages graph attention networks and self-supervised learning. Advanced multichannel microscopy techniques, such as Cyclic Immunofluorescence (CycIF), enable detailed, biomarker-based single-cell mapping, but yield large, densely packed volumes that are difficult to explore. ConGAT implements a machine learning-assisted visual analysis approach for these data. First, ConGAT constructs 3D spatial graphs from volumetric image data and applies a 3D graph attention network to model cell–cell relationships directly in 3D space. Next, we introduce a self-supervised feature refinement strategy that learns discriminative region-of-interest representations without labeled data. Through an interactive visual interface, ConGAT allows experts to define arbitrary combinations of biomarkers, enabling flexible ROIs identification and iterative exploration of spatial patterns. We assess ConGAT on synthetic ground truth and on real-world data. An evaluation with domain expert validation demonstrates that ConGAT identifies spatial patterns and candidate ROIs that show substantial agreement with expert assessments of biological relevance.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104722.title: Adaptive self-refining joint bilateral normal filtering for mesh denoising
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104722.abstract: The bilateral filter has been widely used for decades in various fields, including image processing and mesh denoising. Extending its capabilities, the joint bilateral filter was introduced to incorporate a guidance field, improving filtering quality by leveraging auxiliary information. While joint bilateral filtering guided by surface normals is highly effective for mesh denoising, current approaches rely on globally fixed Gaussian-kernel parameters, inherently limiting their ability to adapt to complex local geometry. In this paper, we propose a fully anisotropic, self-refining joint bilateral normal filtering framework. Our method overcomes global parameter limitations by dynamically estimating per-face spatial and range variances based on local geometric characteristics. Furthermore, we introduce an iterative refinement scheme that progressively updates these variance parameters as mesh normals are filtered, allowing the algorithm to self-adapt during the denoising process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing classical techniques, achieving an average error reduction of approximately 20% compared to baseline guided normal filtering. In addition, the proposed method proved to be effective against a recent optimization method and a tested deep learning approach, while maintaining computational efficiency without requiring offline training datasets.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104732.title: Metric-consistent road-surface novel view synthesis under road-centric sparse-view acquisition
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104732.abstract: Road-surface-centred novel-view synthesis remains challenging under vehicle-mounted acquisition. Near-linear forward motion and grazing-angle observations leave road geometry weakly constrained. Sparse or repetitive texture, reflections, and far-range perspective compression further degrade image correspondence, stereo depth, and photometric optimisation. We formulate this setting as a metric-consistency problem and introduce a three-phase stereo–LiDAR neural rendering framework that keeps metric information explicit from pose estimation to ray-level supervision. The first stage builds a SuperPoint–SuperGlue stereo-temporal graph that combines temporal tracking edges with fixed-baseline stereo edges to improve SfM coverage under forward road motion. The second stage converts RAFT-Stereo disparity into a sensor-supported dense Z-depth prior through online LiDAR-based scale estimation and log-domain residual propagation. The final stage trains Instant-NGP with anchor-distance confidence-weighted structural losses, so completed-depth pixels close to direct LiDAR support impose stronger ray-level constraints than weakly supported regions. On RSRD (Zhao et al., 2023), the pose front end produces full-sequence reconstructions for all 15 evaluated sequences. Under a near-view held-out-frame protocol over six scenes, the confidence-aware renderer achieves 30.25 dB mean PSNR and 0.7883 mean SSIM, and reduces rendered-depth MAE at held-out LiDAR pixels from 1.81 m with RGB-only training to 0.48 m. The depth prior reduces held-out LiDAR sample AbsRel from 0.0141 for RAFT-Stereo with only per-frame metric conversion to 0.0088 after log-domain calibration under a 10% anchor/90% held-out protocol. This held-out LiDAR evaluation measures metric consistency within the same stereo–LiDAR system rather than independent dense-depth accuracy. Together, the results show improved near-view image quality and rendered-depth consistency under road-centric stereo–LiDAR acquisition.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104724.title: Enriching dimensionality reduction with distortion cues
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104724.abstract: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) techniques like t-SNE and UMAP, while powerful visualization tools, inherently introduce distortion during the high-to-low-dimensional mapping process. This distortion means the resulting layout often fails to represent the original high-dimensional distances and relationships faithfully. For instance, visually proximal clusters may be distant in the original space (a global distortion artifact), or densely grouped high-dimensional points may appear scattered (a local density artifact). Prior research consistently shows that practitioners working with DR layouts, especially those less experienced, are frequently unaware of these inherent visual pitfalls, leading them to perform faulty analyses and draw incorrect conclusions based on misleading layouts. To directly address this analytical misuse, this work shows that simple geometry-based layout enrichment mechanisms can substantially prevent misinterpretations. By enriching the structures that surface in the 2D projection with information about their true high-dimensional distances, our approach avoids the approximation errors and smoothness assumptions introduced by typical distortion metrics. We present a Delaunay-based layout enrichment visualization, demonstrating the corrective power of simple distance-based approaches to assist users in their analysis. Furthermore, a comprehensive user evaluation confirms our hypothesis that participants equipped with our enriched layouts exhibit a lower incidence of analytical errors compared to those using established baselines, validating the practical utility of our approach.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104731.title: SRUP-GS:Structure-aware rank and uncertainty-guided perturbation for 3D Gaussian Splatting

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104723.title: Neural oriented boundary detection for particle-based fluids
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104723.abstract: Advancements in computational power have increasingly enabled the application of deep learning to enhance fluid simulation pipelines. In this work, we introduce a multi-task deep learning framework designed to simultaneously address boundary particle detection and normal vector estimation in SPH fluids. Our primary contribution is the Sparse Voxel Fluid Convolutional Neural Network (Sparse VFCNN), an architecture that leverages spatially sparse 3D convolutions to overcome the computational bottlenecks associated with traditional volumetric networks. Developed as an optimized successor to an initial dense architecture (Dense VFCNN), the sparse variant achieves competitive performance with a significant reduction in processing time. Our results demonstrate that the Sparse VFCNN approximates the precision of state-of-the-art methods while providing unified outputs — a feature essential for consistent geometric representation in fluid simulations. Furthermore, the framework is agnostic to the ground-truth data source, allowing for seamless integration with various detection and estimation methods. By combining high efficiency with multi-task learning, the Sparse VFCNN offers a robust and versatile alternative for enhancing geometric fidelity in large-scale fluid simulation frameworks.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104736.title: Faster progressive geometry compression via normal uncertainty
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104736.abstract: Progressive compression of triangle mesh geometry typically exploits spatial coherence to reduce data size while preserving surface detail. In applications where lossy compression is permissible, an effective strategy is to align distortion with the limitations of human visual perception. Existing methods rely on perceptual metrics to steer refinement, but doing so typically incurs additional data overhead to specify where each refinement occurs. We propose a progressive geometry compression algorithm that leverages a perceptually informed model of normal uncertainty to predict where distortion is most likely to be noticeable. This enables the encoder to focus refinements in those regions without explicitly transmitting their locations at each step, thereby reducing overhead. While our initial approach produced reconstructions ranked higher by established perceptual metrics compared to a baseline of Edgebreaker with weighted parallelogram prediction, its high computational cost limited practical deployment. In this extended work, we address this bottleneck by introducing an Adaptive Quasi-Monte Carlo sampling method utilizing a Halton sequence and an early-stopping heuristic. This strategy substantially accelerates the compression pipeline and improves the overall perceptual quality. Furthermore, we explore a neural estimator with the potential to further speed up the normal uncertainty evaluation process. However, while this approach shows potential, further research is required to achieve sufficient accuracy and reliability for practical integration.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104748.title: Photo-reflective sensing for parametric 3D facial expression reconstruction in head-mounted display
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104748.abstract: Reconstructing the 3D facial expressions of head-mounted display (HMD) wearers is essential for natural avatar communication in virtual reality (VR). Camera-based methods achieve high fidelity but require heavy processing and raise privacy concerns. In contrast, non-imaging sensors are lightweight and privacy-preserving, but they provide only sparse features. We propose a reconstruction system that learns high-dimensional 3D facial representations from camera images during training and performs inference using only compact photo-reflective sensors embedded in the HMD. This design combines the expressiveness of camera-based supervision with the efficiency and privacy of sensor-based operation at inference time. Experimental results show that the system reconstructs 3D facial expressions from sensor data alone at inference time. Accuracy improves more from diverse HMD attachment conditions than from additional samples collected under a single attachment condition. A dedicated jaw-pose predictor and lightweight personalization with small wearer-specific datasets further reduce reconstruction error. A sensor ablation experiment further shows that sensor placement within a region is more important than regional coverage, and that glabella and nose sensors are particularly critical for reconstruction. Furthermore, we show that wear-invariant pretraining improves cross-wear robustness under one-set calibration. In this cohort, a calibration analysis identifies informative expression classes and yields a reduced-expression calibration protocol, in which users perform the first K expressions in a cohort-derived common order; with K = 20 , this protocol matches the full 30-expression calibration baseline.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104739.title: Guiding through uncertainties in visual analytics: A survey
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104739.abstract: Several uncertainties emerge in each component of the visual analytics (VA) cycle that hinder the user’s ability to make efficient and effective decisions, e.g., through missing data, model approximations, or visual mappings. Well-known VA strategies aim first at making users aware of these uncertainties, often through visual means. When visuals alone are insufficient to accurately quantify or communicate uncertainties, VA designers may rely on guidance to support users’ understanding of these uncertainties throughout the VA cycle. While prior VA research has attempted to conceptualize guidance, the ability and mechanisms for guidance to comprehensively address different sources of uncertainties remain an open question. In this survey, we characterize the relationships between uncertainties and guidance in VA literature. Our key contribution is a taxonomic framework that relates uncertainty sources to relevant guidance strategies and their respective profiles, i.e., roles, scopes, and features. Through this taxonomy, we discuss how guidance addresses uncertainties, identify research gaps, and promote a more comprehensive understanding of guidance strategies to support effective design for uncertainty in VA. Our survey underscores the effectiveness of guidance in navigating uncertainties with context-aware and multi-scope strategies. We highlight challenging opportunities for further research in this space, especially in the adjacent areas of accessibility and onboarding, and suggest new research areas, such as narrative and persuasion guidance to support uncertainty awareness in VA.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104750.title: Authoring tools for immersive virtual, augmented and mixed reality: A systematic review of content creation platforms, emerging technologies, and their limitations
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104750.abstract: Immersive Reality is increasingly adopted across diverse sectors, including industry, education, and training. However, creating immersive content is frequently identified as a complex task that requires specialized programming skills. This systematic review follows the PRISMA framework to survey the existing literature on authoring tools for immersive Virtual, Augmented, and Mixed Reality, critically analyzing their technical characteristics, integration of emerging technologies, and limitations across 135 eligible studies. The data reveals a strong emphasis on addressing these technical barriers, showing that 116 of the reviewed tools require no programming expertise and utilize visual or demonstrative interactions instead. Regarding interaction, controller-based input is the primary standard (83 studies) due to its precision for complex UI tasks, while hand tracking (41 studies) is also frequently employed to enable direct manipulation. Regarding emerging technologies, the review identifies 28 studies that utilize Artificial Intelligence (AI) to assist users, while digital twins (DTs) and WebXR systems are each featured in 11 studies. Furthermore, a limitation in expressiveness was identified in 84 studies, referring to the degree of functional and representational capacity that a tool supports. In these cases, tools lack sufficient flexibility to implement complex logic, advanced workflows, or custom behaviors, thereby constraining the range of tasks or use cases they can support. Finally, approximately 26% of the analyzed literature is characterized as preliminary studies, with the Training & Simulation sector reporting the highest proportion (40%). Ultimately, this review demonstrates that while most research has focused on making tools easy to use, these solutions still lack functional expressiveness and the ability to handle complex tasks, as well as empirical validation.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104752.title: Human–human joint interaction in Cross-Reality systems: The impact of immersion and synchronicity
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104752.abstract: Performing a Joint Interaction (JI) across the Reality–Virtuality (R-V) continuum remains challenging particularly in enabling shared manipulation of tangible real-world entities from distinct realities. To address this gap, this work investigates how interaction synchronicity and immersion level shape Cross-Reality (CR) JI involving shared manipulation of tangible entities by focusing on their impact on aspects pertaining task perceived presence, perceived workload, sense of inclusion/exclusion, empowerment and perceived control. To support this investigation, an exploratory user study examined human–human CR JI scenarios through the development of three interaction probes: a checkerboard, a comic book, and a music player, each re-creating specific types of JI that enables an Augmented Reality (AR) user and a real-world user to engage with a shared, manipulable entity under varying synchronization conditions. The quantitative results suggest that synchronous interaction enhanced perceived presence, while qualitative accounts pointed to a stronger inclusion and connection. Perceived workload showed differences across immersion conditions, with qualitative findings further highlighting the role of interaction constraints and control distribution in shaping participants’ experiences. Overall, effective CR JI design requires balancing physical and virtual affordances while enabling meaningful participation across asymmetric realities. These insights are synthesized into initial design implications for future CR JI systems, providing guidance for interaction approaches that support meaningful participation, awareness, and coordination across heterogeneous realities.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104751.title: IBMM++: Improved and versatile motion generation with implicit Bézier curves
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104751.abstract: Creating high-quality character animation remains an intricate and cumbersome process. Recently, diffusion models have unlocked the ability to generate diverse movements from high-level condition signals such as text. For artist-friendly control, motion diffusion leveraging Bézier curves have been shown to allow precise joint-level conditioning. Yet, these works have been limited to joints at a fixed temporal stride, while animators require more temporal flexibility when keyframing or manipulating tangents to achieve animation principles such as easing in & out. In Vögeli et al. we presented a new Implicit Bézier Motion Model (IBMM), which during training is exposed to all possible configurations of control points, enabling control at arbitrary timings. In addition, we introduced a new quantitative measure of ease-in and -out, which leads to a novel condition over the motion generation process to reflect this artistic principle. In this extended version (IBMM++), we further improve constraint accuracy, reduce foot sliding, and enable motion extension, orientation constraints, longer sequences, and stable iterative editing through architectural updates, a revised tangent formulation, a randomized constraint sampling strategy, and dedicated inference-time methods, validated on a larger internal dataset with more varied motions.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104775.title: Pano-to-3D: Multi-view consistent 3D indoor scene reconstruction from a single panorama image
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104775.abstract: Single-view scene reconstruction presents significant challenges due to the limited viewpoint information. Panorama images, as a form of image representation with a 360° field of view (FoV), offer a richer source of information for scene reconstruction. Therefore, more and more work utilizes a single panorama image for scene reconstruction. However, existing methods for scene reconstruction from a single panorama image often fail to adequately address the unique characteristics of panorama images and overlook the distinctions between panorama and limited FoV images. In this paper, we propose a novel method for inpainting and reconstructing scenes from a single panorama image. By capitalizing on the distinctive projection characteristics of panorama images and the irregularity of inpainting regions, we develop a panorama inpainting algorithm that incorporates a specialized inpainting strategy and fine-tunes a diffusion model to enhance the quality of inpainting for a single image. Additionally, we exploit the consistency of existing geometry to establish a multi-view consistent denoising process, ensuring coherence among images captured from different viewpoints. Through our two-stage inpainting strategy, we successfully transform the scene geometry derived from a single panorama image into a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method compared to state-of-the-art single-view scene reconstruction methods.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104772.title: Glyph-based visualization with highlighting for analyzing longitudinal machine learning experiments
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104772.abstract: Parameter tuning represents a complex and laborious challenge in machine learning (ML), primarily due to the often opaque interactions among multiple parameters. Recognizing this challenge, ML researchers explore a long-term experimental approach to investigate relationships among parameters. Multivariate visualization techniques offer valuable support for such analyses. In this work, we explore a glyph-based visualization approach to support domain experts in analyzing experimental results, using neural network pruning as a specific investigative scenario. Compared to other multivariate visualization methods, glyphs are well suited to representing heterogeneous data types and multiple variables within a compact visual form. However, the large number of variables involved in parameter exploration can push the limits of what a single glyph can effectively encode. To address this issue, we introduce glyph highlighting to direct users’ analytical focus to relevant aspects for a specific experiment. To guide the design of glyph highlighting, we extend established glyph design criteria to the highlighting context and propose the concept of a glyph ID alphabet, which enables highlighting to be considered and assessed in a manner consistent with encoding ordinary data variables. We evaluated our method through case studies and expert interviews. We further conducted semi-structured interviews with ML researchers to collect comparative feedback on the effectiveness of glyph-based visualization.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104773.title: Exploring personalization in eXtended reality stroke rehabilitation: Proposal of assessment dimensions and preliminary user studies
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104773.abstract: Rehabilitation plays a critical role in stroke recovery, enabling individuals to regain lost functions and reintegrate daily routines. However, conventional programs often adopt standardized approaches that overlook individual characteristics, preferences, and recovery pace. This lack of personalization can reduce engagement, diminish motivation, and ultimately hinder therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in eXtended Reality (XR) offer promising opportunities to address these limitations by enabling the creation of immersive, adaptive environments tailored to the specific needs of each stroke survivor. Despite this, a key challenge remains: how to evaluate the impact of personalization within XR-based rehabilitation experiences. This work addresses this gap through an analysis of 41 publications from the SCOPUS database (2020–2026), with a focus on evaluation methodologies. The review reveals a clear lack of standardized instruments capable of capturing personalization effects. To address this, we adopt a Human-Centered Design (HCD) approach involving domain experts, healthcare professionals, and stroke survivors to identify core dimensions of XR-based personalization. These dimensions inform the development of questionnaire items intended for post-task evaluation. These items were applied in two user studies with distinct XR-Personalized systems, involving a total of 50 participants. Results support the feasibility of the proposed evaluation approach and provide an initial exploration of how personalization influences user experience, contributing to the development of more effective evaluation instruments for XR-based rehabilitation interventions

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104783.title: A reflective case study of long-term visualization system evolution: Evidence from booktracker
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104783.abstract: BookTracker is a visualization platform developed through a long-term collaboration with historians to support research on the provenance records of early printed books in the Material Evidence in Incunabula (MEI) database. Over several years, the project expanded from trajectory-oriented views for tracing individual copies to a family of visualization tools supporting the exploration and comparison of provenance records, the interpretation of incomplete evidence, and the analysis of ownership relationships. In this paper, we revisit these developments as a reflective synthesis of platform evolution across multiple sub-projects, rather than as a single bounded and project-specific design study. By examining how new domain questions, changing contributors, and recurring data challenges shaped successive systems, we identify a set of planning considerations for long-term interdisciplinary visualization work. These include recognizing when emerging analytical questions warrant branching into new tools, maintaining coherence across task-specific visualizations built on shared data, adapting visual representations and interactions to changing units of analysis, and supporting knowledge transfer across collaborators and student developers. Our contribution is an experience-based, cross-project account of concerns that become more visible when visualization work unfolds across years, contributors, and partially independent systems. We show how such long-term cases can complement established design study thinking by surfacing practical considerations for sustaining meaningful visualization support over time.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104782.title: Gaussian splatting for surface reconstruction: A survey
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104782.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient volumetric representation for 3D reconstruction from images, enabling high-fidelity novel-view synthesis with real-time rendering. However, recovering accurate surfaces from splat primitives remains challenging because the original formulation prioritizes photometric accuracy over geometric consistency. This survey reviews recent methods addressing this limitation. The dominant paradigm estimates regularized depth and normal maps through volume splatting and reconstructs meshes via truncated signed distance function (TSDF) fusion. Alternative directions include continuous opacity-field formulations, hybrid Gaussian–implicit approaches that couple splats with SDFs, and differentiable mesh-in-the-loop optimization frameworks. We further derive Gaussian splatting from the classical ordinary differential equation (ODE) for volume rendering and discuss geometry-oriented extensions of the formulation. We organize the literature into a taxonomy based on primitive design, rendering formulation, geometric supervision, and surface-extraction strategy. We also compare representative methods on the DTU and Tanks and Temples datasets, highlighting trade-offs between reconstruction quality, computational efficiency, and scalability. Finally, we discuss open challenges, including large-scale scene reconstruction, thin-structure recovery, sparse-view robustness, and the need for high-precision benchmarks.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104835.title: STINT: Explanation and visualization of feature interactions for domain experts
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104835.abstract: AI models excel at capturing complex relationships between features, yet many explainable AI ( XAI ) methods overlook this by visualizing each feature in isolation. Although newer techniques can show higher-order interactions, they are often designed for machine learning (ML) experts rather than domain specialists. Our tool, STINT , addresses this gap by providing intuitive visualizations of feature interactions - up to higher orders - using a novel method for computing and displaying feature-group interactions. Drawing on visualization-for-communication research, we create interactive explanations that intuitively convey these interactions to domain experts. Our tool displays interactions both within the model and directly in the data. We evaluate the tool’s effectiveness through case studies and a user study with experts from three domains. With STINT , domain experts gain accessible insight into feature interactions.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104808.title: An adaptive AI-driven virtual reality simulation for de-escalation training in law enforcement: A mixed-methods study
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104808.abstract: De-escalation is a critical communication skill for law enforcement, yet scenario-based training is difficult to scale and often provides limited opportunities for repeatable, reviewable practice. We present an adaptive AI-driven VR de-escalation training system that connects open-ended trainee dialogue, rubric-guided utterance scoring, virtual-subject state changes, and trainer-facing dashboard review. In a mixed-methods study with 14 law enforcement trainees and five trainers, we examined usability, workload, learner perceptions, trainer feedback, and dashboard traces from two simulation attempts. Trainees reported high usability and low workload, and described the system as a lower-pressure space for practicing communication before live role-play. Interaction traces revealed careful de-escalatory trajectories, mixed recovery after low-scoring utterances, and deliberate boundary testing, showing how turn-level scores and transcripts can make conversational consequences visible for debriefing. Trainers valued the system as a rehearsal and coaching tool, while identifying requirements for richer embodiment, trainer visibility, scenario coverage, constraints on AI response variability, and calibration of automated scoring with instructor judgment. This article extends our AIxVR 2026 conference paper while retaining the original study data. Findings position adaptive AI-driven VR as a trainer-mediated rehearsal-and-review environment for high-stakes communication training, not as a standalone measure of trainee competence.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104804.title: Football for all: Towards procedural spatial audio for blind and low-vision spectators
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104804.abstract: This paper describes Football for All , a modular system that transforms football broadcast video into an immersive, headphone-based spatial audio experience for blind and low-vision (BLV) spectators. The system integrates: (i) a computer vision pipeline for detecting and tracking players and the ball, estimating pitch calibration, and converting image detections into pitch coordinates; (ii) a dense action spotting module that temporally localizes ball-related events with strict 1-second precision; and (iii) a Unity-based logic engine that processes a structured game-state stream and generates procedurally created 3D spatial audio using head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) and head tracking. The audio engine renders in real time, but the current prototype is not yet a live system: the computer-vision stage processes pre-recorded broadcast footage sequentially to preserve identity consistency, and end-to-end latency has not yet been measured. The design supports robust post-processing under occlusions and viewpoint changes, and an event-to-sound audio lexicon that reduces listener cognitive load by mapping football semantics to distinct acoustic cues.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104803.title: Enumeration of reference-foldable origami shapes and its application to silhouette quiz design
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104803.abstract: We present an algorithm for enumerating origami folded shapes that can be folded accurately by referencing visible landmarks. Prior enumeration work generates all geometrically consistent folded shapes for a given number of fold operations, but many of those shapes require folds whose reference landmarks (corners or edges) are hidden beneath upper layers and therefore invisible during actual folding. Such folds can still be made physically, but only as judgment folds ( gurai-ori ), placed by eye at an approximate position, so the resulting silhouette cannot be reproduced exactly. Our algorithm augments the enumeration with a reference foldability test: before accepting a fold, it checks that every landmark used to specify the fold line is visible to the folder, and that the fold outcome (point coincidence or edge alignment) is genuinely achievable given which paper regions move. We define per-operation visibility conditions for the three origami axioms commonly used in simple origami, together with a consistency check for folds that move the entire sheet. Applied to a square sheet with up to four folds, the algorithm yields a reference-foldable set strictly smaller than the geometrically consistent set. We demonstrate an application to origami silhouette quiz design, whose rules admit only landmark-referenced folds: filtering guarantees that every designed quiz can be folded exactly under its own rules, and path-count-based difficulty estimates are computed under the same rule set that the solver uses.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104817.title: GameRule Studio: A visual no-code environment for rule-based multi-agent systems in video games
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104817.abstract: This paper presents GameRule Studio, a no-code visual authoring environment for Unity built on the existing GameRule architecture and domain-specific language. It supports scene configuration, actor properties, and reactive when-do rules through contextual controls and bidirectional conversion between visual representations and supported JSON descriptors. Evaluation combines technical equivalence, a moderated user study, import robustness, controlled-scale measurements, and inspection of behavior representations. Eight controlled descriptor pairs and three complete game-project pairs passed 44/44 comparisons of canonical JSON, ordered parsed representations, normalized generated C#, and round trips. Three targeted runtime tests passed, yielding 47/47 checks overall. Fifteen participants completed 60/60 tasks, 46/60 without task-specific guidance, and produced correct behaviors on 54/60 first Play attempts. Mean System Usability Scale score was 95.3/100 (SD = 5.0), and mean unweighted NASA Task Load Index score was 15.6/100 (SD = 8.1). Six fault-injection cases exposed import limitations: malformed JSON was rejected, whereas five syntactically valid but invalid descriptors were accepted without import-time diagnostics. All 25 measured samples across five scale configurations preserved predefined correctness properties. Median time for import, exhaustive actor-panel reconstruction, and export increased from 1.07 s for 10 actors with 10 rules each to 32.03 s for 200 actors with 20 rules each. Inspection of 41 actor declarations and 107 rules documented repetition and auxiliary-state patterns. Results support technical equivalence within the tested scope and indicate high perceived usability and low reported workload in the studied sample, while identifying import-validation and editor-scaling limitations. Comparative authoring benefits and cross-engine operation remain untested.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104827.title: LLMVisExplorer: Visually exploring the knowledge landscape of large language models
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104827.abstract: The performance of large language models (LLMs) in specific knowledge domains is often evaluated based on question and answer (Q&A) benchmark datasets. Although benchmark reports sometimes include domain-level breakdowns, evaluation results are still frequently summarized through aggregate accuracy values or coarse tables that make it difficult to inspect multi-level, multi-metric, and question-level performance variation. This is problematic because Q&A benchmark datasets are by design diverse and span broad domains, such as science (SciQ) or biomedicine (PubMedQA). We argue that overly coarse evaluation summaries can collapse meaningful details: strong performance in easier or overrepresented areas can overshadow weaknesses in critical or complex subdomains, making such summaries insufficient for downstream use. To enable better understanding of real-world model capabilities essential for downstream applications, we propose LLMVisExplorer, an interactive visualization system that facilitates in-depth evaluation of LLM performance within the subdomains of complex knowledge domains. Based on LLM evaluation design requirements grounded in the natural language processing (NLP) literature, LLMVisExplorer bridges the gap between coarse-grained benchmark reporting and actionable model insights by enabling multifaceted, visually guided performance analysis across hierarchical knowledge domains. It empowers both, LLM developers and LLM users, to identify domain-specific strengths and weaknesses, in order to inform model development, red-teaming, and deployment decisions. We discuss LLMVisExplorer’s design requirements as well as its realization, and showcase its potential on several use cases evaluating single models as well as comparing multiple models, such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Yi-large. LLMVisExplorer’s source code and data will be provided upon acceptance.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104813.title: KineBridge: Bridging sparse constraints and foundation motion priors
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104813.abstract: Sparse pose keyframes together with a full root trajectory provide direct geometric control for human motion authoring, but the transitions between pose constraints remain inherently ambiguous. Task-specific generators must learn both constraint alignment and a broad motion distribution from limited control data, which often leads to over-smoothed transitions or local artifacts. We present KineBridge, a geometric-control framework built on the pretrained HY-Motion 1.0 generator. The foundation backbone remains frozen, while a parallel trainable branch converts masked pose and trajectory conditions into a temporally aligned control sequence. The branch separately encodes the two modalities, applies Sparse-KV, Dense-Query attention according to their validity masks, and uses bidirectional fusion to couple articulated pose with root-trajectory context. Zero-initialized residual blocks then inject the condition tokens throughout the frozen double-stream and single-stream Transformer stages. The original text inputs are replaced with the pretrained model’s fixed null text features, enabling the model to focus on geometric control while retaining the pretrained motion prior. On the HumanML3D/CombatMotion test split, KineBridge achieves the best MPJPE, Anchor MPJPE, FID, and diversity among the compared systems, while PMG remains stronger in trajectory consistency. On the cross-dataset AIST++ evaluation, it achieves the best keyframe-alignment, bone-length, foot-sliding, ground-penetration, and diversity results. Component and injection-frequency ablations further validate sparse-aware propagation, pose–trajectory fusion, and layer-wise residual conditioning. These results demonstrate that precise sparse-pose control can be integrated into a frozen foundation motion model without retraining the backbone.

10.1016/j.cag.2026.104837.title: Towards calibration-robust evaluation of 6-DoF head motion prediction: Kinematic and graphic implications for EdgeXR
10.1016/j.cag.2026.104837.abstract: Accurate six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) head-motion prediction is essential for compensating motion-to-photon latency in extended reality (XR) systems, but predictor evaluation often depends on external ground truth whose residual spatial and temporal calibration errors can be mistaken for forecasting error. We present a calibration-robust learning and evaluation pipeline based on body-frame motion increments and perturbation-aware robustness metrics, including Calibration Sensitivity Slopes (CSS) and robust area under the curve ( A U C rob ). Compared with earlier work, this work broadens the corruption analysis to include translation offset, lever-arm perturbation, and temporal skew; validates the protocol on XRPoseSync, where motion-capture (MoCap) poses are calibrated into the head-mounted display (HMD) tracking space with natural residual disagreement; and introduces a Unity-based rendering analysis that maps trajectory-level robustness to depth-conditioned screen-space reprojection error Results show that across the tested architectures, body-frame targets yield lower bias-weighted translational RMSE than world-frame targets at each evaluated XRPoseSync horizon; for GRU, the reduction is 21%–29%. No systematic body-frame advantage is observed under noise- or drift-weighted residual conditions. In representative matched-depth Unity replays, body-frame predictions also yield slightly lower total near-field reprojection error, an effect that matters for AR registration, where translational pose errors are amplified by perspective projection. The proposed protocol provides a practical methodology for benchmarking calibration-robust XR predictors when real-world residual calibration error is difficult to measure directly.

10.1016/s0097-8493(96)00079-9.title: Optimal static 2-dimensional screen subdivision for parallel rasterization architectures
10.1016/s0097-8493(96)00079-9.abstract: Designers of computer graphics hardware have used increasing device counts available from IC manufacturers to increase parallelism using techniques such as putting a longer pipeline of data path elements on integrated circuits, or developing designs which use an array of processors. Pixel-Planes 1–5 and PixelFlow‡ are examples of architectures which use an array of pixel processors for rasterization. Early generations of Pixel-Planes attempted to make these arrays as large as the display providing one processor for each display pixel. Later generations improved performance by grouping processors into multiple smaller arrays, subdividing the screen into sections of a corresponding size and having the arrays independently process the screen subdivisions. This paper describes simulations which were performed to determine the optimum size subdivision for a graphics computer which uses Pixel-Planes type parallelism, i.e. static two dimensional screen subdivision parallel polygon rasterization. We then develop a mathematical approach to determining the optimal subdivision size and show that it agrees well with the experimental data. For special purpose architectures we show that the optimal size depends not only on the polygon size but also on the silicon area consumed by the rasterizer overhead. The mathematical approach can be directly applied to special purpose architectures, and we show how it can be modified for use in analyzing algorithms developed for general purpose architectures such as the Intel Touchstone or Paragon, or the Thinking Machines CM-5.

10.1016/s0097-8493(97)00011-3.title: A spring force formulation for elastically deformable models
10.1016/s0097-8493(97)00011-3.abstract: Continuous deformable models are generally represented using a grid of control points. The elastic properties are then modeled using the interactions between these points. The formulations based on elasticity theory express these interactions using stiffness matrices. These matrices store the elastic properties of the models and they should be evolved in time according to changing elastic properties of the models. However, forming the stiffness matrices at any step of an animation is very difficult and sometimes the differential equations that should be solved to produce animation become ill-conditioned. Instead of modeling the elasticities using stiffness matrices, the interactions between model points could be expressed in terms of external spring forces. In this paper, a spring force formulation for animating elastically deformable models is presented. In this formulation, elastic properties of the materials are represented as external spring forces as opposed to forming complicated stiffness matrices. (C) 1997 Elsevier Science Ltd.

10.1016/s0097-8493(99)00103-x.abstract: We describe an experimental mobile augmented reality system (MARS) testbed that employs different user interfaces to allow outdoor and indoor users to access and manage information that is spatially registered with the real world. Outdoor users can experience spatialized multimedia presentations that are presented on a head-tracked, see-through, head-worn display used in conjunction with a hand-held pen-based computer. Indoor users can get an overview of the outdoor scene and communicate with outdoor users through a desktop user interface or a head- and hand-tracked immersive augmented reality user interface.

10.1016/s0097-8493(99)00091-6.title: Hierarchical back-face computation
10.1016/s0097-8493(99)00091-6.abstract: Abstract We present a sub-linear algorithm to compute the set of back-facing polygons in a polyhedral model. The algorithm partitions the model into hierarchical clusters based on the orientations and positions of the polygons. As a pre-processing step, the algorithm constructs spatial decompositions with respect to each cluster. For a sequence of back-face computations, the algorithm exploits the coherence in view-point movement to efficiently determine whether it is in front of or behind a cluster. Due to coherence, the algorithm's expected running time is linear in the number of clusters on average. We have applied this algorithm to speed up the rendering of polyhedral models. On average, we are able to cull about 40% of the polygons. The algorithm accounts for 5% of the total CPU time per frame on an SGI Onyx. The overall frame rate is improved by 40–75% as compared to the standard back-face culling implemented in hardware. We also present an extension of our back-face computation algorithm to determine silhouettes of polygonal models. Our technique finds true perspective silhouettes by collecting edges at the common boundaries of back-facing and front-facing clusters.

10.1109/2945.468400.title: Optical models for direct volume rendering
10.1109/2945.468400.abstract: This tutorial survey paper reviews several different models for light interaction with volume densities of absorbing, glowing, reflecting, and/or scattering material. They are, in order of increasing realism, absorption only, emission only, emission and absorption combined, single scattering of external illumination without shadows, single scattering with shadows, and multiple scattering. For each model the paper provides the physical assumptions, describes the applications for which it is appropriate, derives the differential or integral equations for light transport, presents calculation methods for solving them, and shows output images for a data set representing a cloud. Special attention is given to calculation methods for the multiple scattering model.>

10.1109/2945.466717.title: Collision detection for interactive graphics applications
10.1109/2945.466717.abstract: Collision detection and response are important for interactive graphics applications such as vehicle simulators and virtual reality. Unfortunately, previous collision detection algorithms are too slow for interactive use. The paper presents a new algorithm for rigid or articulated objects that meets performance goals through a form of time critical computing. The algorithm supports progressive refinement, detecting collisions between successively tighter approximations to object surfaces as the application allows it more processing time. The algorithm uses simple four dimensional geometry to approximate motion, and hierarchies of spheres to approximate three dimensional surfaces at multiple resolutions. In a sample application, the algorithm allows interactive performance that is not possible with a good previous algorithm. In particular, the new algorithm provides acceptable accuracy while maintaining a steady and high frame rate, which in some cases improves on the previous algorithm's rate by more than two orders of magnitude.>

10.1109/2945.468391.title: Visualizing network data
10.1109/2945.468391.abstract: Networks are critical to modern society, and a thorough understanding of how they behave is crucial to their efficient operation. Fortunately, data on networks is plentiful; by visualizing this data, it is possible to greatly improve our understanding. Our focus is on visualizing the data associated with a network and not on simply visualizing the structure of the network itself. We begin with three static network displays; two of these use geographical relationships, while the third is a matrix arrangement that gives equal emphasis to all network links. Static displays can be swamped with large amounts of data; hence we introduce direct manipulation techniques that permit the graphs to continue to reveal relationships in the context of much more data. In effect, the static displays are parameterized so that interesting views may easily be discovered interactively. The software to carry out this network visualization is called SeeNet.>

10.1109/2945.537309.title: Glyphs for visualizing uncertainty in vector fields
10.1109/2945.537309.abstract: Environmental data have inherent uncertainty which is often ignored in visualization. Meteorological stations and doppler radars, including their time series averages, have a wealth of uncertainty information that traditional vector visualization methods such as meteorological wind barbs and arrow glyphs simply ignore. We have developed a new vector glyph to visualize uncertainty in winds and ocean currents. Our approach is to include uncertainty in direction and magnitude, as well as the mean direction and length, in vector glyph plots. Our glyph shows the variation in uncertainty, and provides fair comparisons of data from instruments, models, and time averages of varying certainty. We also define visualizations that incorporate uncertainty in an unambiguous manner as verity visualization. We use both quantitative and qualitative methods to compare our glyphs to traditional ones. Subjective comparison tests with experts are provided, as well as objective tests, where the information density of our new glyphs and traditional glyphs are compared. The design of the glyph and numerous examples using environmental data are given. We show enhanced visualizations, data together with their uncertainty information, that may improve understanding of environmental vector field data quality.

10.1109/2945.489389.title: D-NURBS: a physics-based framework for geometric design
10.1109/2945.489389.abstract: Presents dynamic non-uniform rational B-splines (D-NURBS), a physics-based generalization of NURBS. NURBS have become a de facto standard in commercial modeling systems. Traditionally, however, NURBS have been viewed as purely geometric primitives, which require the designer to interactively adjust many degrees of freedom-control points and associated weights-to achieve the desired shapes. The conventional shape modification process can often be clumsy and laborious. D-NURBS are physics-based models that incorporate physical quantities into the NURBS geometric substrate. Their dynamic behavior, resulting from the numerical integration of a set of nonlinear differential equations, produces physically meaningful, and hence intuitive shape variation. Consequently, a modeler can interactively sculpt complex shapes to required specifications not only in the traditional indirect fashion, by adjusting control points and setting weights, but also through direct physical manipulation, by applying simulated forces and local and global shape constraints. We use Lagrangian mechanics to formulate the equations of motion for D-NURBS curves, tensor-product D-NURBS surfaces, swung D-NURBS surfaces and triangular D-NURBS surfaces. We apply finite element analysis to reduce these equations to efficient numerical algorithms computable at interactive rates on common graphics workstations. We implement a prototype modeling environment based on D-NURBS and demonstrate that D-NURBS can be effective tools in a wide range of computer-aided geometric design (CAGD) applications.

10.1109/2945.468392.title: Real time responsive animation with personality
10.1109/2945.468392.abstract: Building on principles from prior work on procedural texture synthesis (K. Perlin, 1985), we are able to create remarkably lifelike, responsively animated characters in real time. Rhythmic and stochastic noise functions are used to define time varying parameters that drive computer generated puppets. Because we are conveying just the "texture" of motion, we are able to avoid computation of dynamics and constraint solvers. The subjective impression of dynamics and other subtle influences on motion can be conveyed with great visual realism by properly tuned expressions containing pseudo random noise functions. For example, we can make a character appear to be dynamically balancing herself, to appear nervous, or to be gesturing in a particular way. Each move has an internal rhythm, and transitions between moves are temporally constrained so that "impossible" transitions are precluded. For example, if while the character is walking we specify a dance turn, the character will always step into the turn onto the correct weight bearing foot. An operator can make a character perform a properly connected sequence of actions, while conveying particular moods and attitudes, merely by pushing buttons at a high level. Potential uses of such high level "textural" approaches to computer graphic simulation include role playing games, simulated conferences, "clip animation", graphical front ends for MUDs, and synthetic performances.>

10.1109/2945.537306.title: A digital brain atlas for surgical planning, model-driven segmentation, and teaching
10.1109/2945.537306.abstract: We developed a three-dimensional (3D) digitized atlas of the human brain to visualize spatially complex structures. It was designed for use with magnetic resonance (MR) imaging data sets. Thus far, we have used this atlas for surgical planning, model-driven segmentation, and teaching. We used a combination of automated and supervised segmentation methods to define regions of interest based on neuroanatomical knowledge. We also used 3D surface rendering techniques to create a brain atlas that would allow us to visualize complex 3D brain structures. We further linked this Information to script files in order to preserve both spatial information and neuroanatomical knowledge. We present here the application of the atlas for visualization in surgical planning far model-driven segmentation and for the teaching of neuroanatomy. This digitized human brain has the potential to provide important reference information for the planning of surgical procedures. It can also serve as a powerful teaching tool, since spatial relationships among neuroanatomical structures can be more readily envisioned when the user is able to view and rotate the structures in 3D space. Moreover, each element of the brain atlas is associated with a name tag, displayed by a user controlled pointer. The atlas holds a major promise as a template for model-driven segmentation. Using this technique, many regions of interest can be characterized simultaneously on new brain images.

10.1109/2945.556502.title: Image metamorphosis with scattered feature constraints
10.1109/2945.556502.abstract: This paper describes an image metamorphosis technique to handle scattered feature constraints specified with points, polylines, and splines. Solutions to the following three problems are presented: feature specification, warp generation, and transition control. We demonstrate the use of snakes to reduce the burden of feature specification. Next, we propose the use of multilevel free-form deformations (MFFD) to compute C/sup 2/-continuous and one-to-one mapping functions among the specified features. The resulting technique, based on B-spline approximation, is simpler and faster than previous warp generation methods. Furthermore, it produces smooth image transformations without undesirable ripples and foldovers. Finally, we simplify the MFFD algorithm to derive transition functions to control geometry and color blending. Implementation details are furnished and comparisons among various metamorphosis techniques are presented.

10.1109/2945.597796.title: Tracking and visualizing turbulent 3D features
10.1109/2945.597796.abstract: Visualizing 3D time-varying fluid datasets is difficult because of the immense amount of data to be processed and understood. These datasets contain many evolving amorphous regions, and it is difficult to observe patterns and visually follow regions of interest. In this paper, we present a technique which isolates and tracks full-volume representations of regions of interest from 3D regular and curvilinear computational fluid dynamics datasets. Connected voxel regions ("features") are extracted from each time step and matched to features in subsequent time steps. Spatial overlap is used to determine the matching. The features from each time step are stored in octree forests to speed up the matching process. Once the features have been identified and tracked, the properties of the features and their evolutionary history can be computed. This information can be used to enhance isosurface visualization and volume rendering by color coding individual regions. We demonstrate the algorithm on four 3D time-varying simulations from ongoing research in computational fluid dynamics and show how tracking can significantly improve and facilitate the processing of massive datasets.

10.1109/2945.485620.title: Exploiting triangulated surface extraction using tetrahedral decomposition
10.1109/2945.485620.abstract: Beginning with digitized volumetric data, we wish to rapidly and efficiently extract and represent surfaces defined as isosurfaces in the interpolated data. The Marching Cubes algorithm is a standard approach to this problem. We instead perform a decomposition of each 8-cell associated with a voxel into five tetrahedra. We guarantee the resulting surface representation to be closed and oriented, defined by a valid triangulation of the surface of the body, which in turn is presented as a collection of tetrahedra. The entire surface is "wrapped" by a collection of triangles, which form a graph structure, and where each triangle is contained within a single tetrahedron. The representation is similar to the homology theory that uses simplices embedded in a manifold to define a closed curve within each tetrahedron. We introduce data structures based upon a new encoding of the tetrahedra that are at least four times more compact than the standard data structures using vertices and triangles. For parallel computing and improved cache performance, the vertex information is stored local to the tetrahedra. We can distribute the vertices in such a way that no tetrahedron ever contains more than one vertex, We give methods to evaluate surface curvatures and principal directions at each vertex, whenever these quantities are defined. Finally, we outline a method for simplifying the surface, that is reducing the vertex count while preserving the geometry. We compare the characteristics of our methods with an 8-cell based method, and show results of surface extractions from CT-scans and MR-scans at full resolution.

10.1109/2945.597794.title: Conveying the 3D shape of smoothly curving transparent surfaces via texture
10.1109/2945.597794.abstract: Transparency can be a useful device for depicting multiple overlapping surfaces in a single image. The challenge is to render the transparent surfaces in such a way that their 3D shape can be readily understood and their depth distance from underlying structures clearly perceived. This paper describes our investigations into the use of sparsely-distributed discrete, opaque texture as an artistic device for more explicitly indicating the relative depth of a transparent surface and for communicating the essential features of its 3D shape in an intuitively meaningful and minimally occluding way. The driving application for this work is the visualization of layered surfaces in radiation therapy treatment planning data, and the technique is illustrated on transparent isointensity surfaces of radiation dose. We describe the perceptual motivation and artistic inspiration for defining a stroke texture that is locally oriented in the direction of greatest normal curvature (and in which individual strokes are of a length proportional to the magnitude of the curvature in the direction they indicate), and we discuss two alternative methods for applying this texture to isointensity surfaces defined in a volume. We propose an experimental paradigm for objectively measuring observers' ability to judge the shape and depth of a layered transparent surface, in the course of a task which is relevant to the needs of radiotherapy treatment planning, and use this paradigm to evaluate the practical effectiveness of our approach through a controlled observer experiment based on images generated from actual clinical data.

10.1109/2945.468404.title: A predictor-corrector technique for visualizing unsteady flow
10.1109/2945.468404.abstract: Presents a method for visualizing unsteady flow by displaying its vortices. The vortices are identified by using a vorticity-predictor pressure-corrector scheme that follows vortex cores.
